section.title: David's Census and the Altar
section.sectionRationale: The book ends where atonement is made. David sins by numbering his fighting men, apparently trusting in his military strength; a plague follows, and David, the shepherd, pleads that judgment fall on him rather than the sheep. At the LORD's word he builds an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah, refusing to offer what costs him nothing, and the plague is halted. That very threshing floor becomes the site of the temple, so the book closes at the place of sacrifice and mercy, pointing to the greater atonement to come.
section.thesis: David's proud census brings judgment, but when he confesses his sin and, as shepherd, offers himself for the sheep, God's great mercy halts the plague through sacrifice on the threshing floor that will become the temple mount, so that 2 Samuel closes at the place of costly atonement, where wrath is stayed and mercy triumphs, pointing to the cross.
section.frameNote: Three beats: David's census and his stricken conscience, verses 1 to 10; the choice of judgment and the plague, verses 11 to 17; and the altar on Araunah's threshing floor where the plague is halted, verses 18 to 25.

verses.text: Again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He stirred up David against them, saying, “Go and take a census of Israel and Judah.”
So the king said to Joab the commander of his army, who was with him, “Go now throughout the tribes of Israel from Dan to Beersheba and register the troops, so that I may know their number.”
But Joab replied to the king, “May the LORD your God multiply the troops a hundred times over, and may the eyes of my lord the king see it. But why does my lord the king want to do such a thing?”

Nevertheless, the king’s word prevailed against Joab and against the commanders of the army. So Joab and the commanders of the army departed from the presence of the king to register the troops of Israel.
They crossed the Jordan and camped near Aroer, south of the town in the middle of the valley, and proceeded toward Gad and Jazer.
Then they went to Gilead and the land of Tahtim-hodshi, and on to Dan-jaan and around to Sidon.
They went toward the fortress of Tyre and all the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites. Finally, they went on to the Negev of Judah, to Beersheba.
At the end of nine months and twenty days, having gone through the whole land, they returned to Jerusalem.
And Joab reported to the king the total number of the troops. In Israel there were 800,000 men of valor who drew the sword, and in Judah there were 500,000.

After David had numbered the troops, his conscience was stricken and he said to the LORD, “I have {{chata|sinned}} greatly in what I have done. Now, O LORD, I beg You to take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.”

units.label: The plague and the shepherd's plea
units.note: let Your hand fall upon me

verses.text: When David got up in the morning, the word of the LORD had come to Gad the prophet, David’s seer:
“Go and tell David that this is what the LORD says: ‘I am offering you three options. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you.’”

So Gad went and said to David, “Do you choose to endure three years of famine in your land, three months of fleeing the pursuit of your enemies, or three days of plague upon your land? Now then, think it over and decide how I should reply to Him who sent me.”
David answered Gad, “I am deeply distressed. Please, let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for His {{rachamim|mercies}} are great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men.”
So the LORD sent a plague upon Israel from that morning until the appointed time, and seventy thousand of the people from Dan to Beersheba died.

But when the angel stretched out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, the LORD relented from the calamity and said to the angel who was destroying the people, “Enough! Withdraw your hand now!” At that time the angel of the LORD was by the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

When David saw the angel striking down the people, he said to the LORD, “Surely I, the shepherd, have sinned and acted wickedly. But these sheep, what have they done? Please, let Your hand fall upon me and my father’s house.”

units.label: The altar on the threshing floor
units.note: I will not offer what costs me nothing

verses.text: And that day Gad came to David and said to him, “Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”
So David went up at the word of Gad, just as the LORD had commanded.
When Araunah looked out and saw the king and his servants coming toward him, he went out and bowed facedown before the king.
“Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” Araunah said. “To buy your threshing floor,” David replied, “that I may build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague upon the people may be halted.”
Araunah said to David, “May my lord the king take whatever seems good to him and offer it up. Here are the oxen for a burnt offering and the threshing sledges and ox yokes for the wood.
O king, Araunah gives all these to the king.” He also said to the king, “May the LORD your God accept you.”

“No,” replied the king, “I insist on paying a price, for I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
And there he built an altar to the LORD and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the LORD answered the prayers on behalf of the land, and the plague upon Israel was halted.

chata.gloss: To sin, to miss the mark, to offend against God. After the census David's conscience strikes him and he confesses, 'I have sinned greatly,' begging the LORD to take away his iniquity. As with Bathsheba, David's greatness is not that he never sinned but that, convicted, he confesses honestly and casts himself on God's mercy.

rachamim.gloss: Compassion, tender mercies, deep pity; related to the word for womb, evoking a parent's yearning love. Facing judgment, David chooses to fall into the hand of the LORD, 'for His mercies are great,' trusting God's rachamim rather than the mercilessness of men. The plague is halted precisely because the LORD relents in compassion, showing that His mercy tempers His judgment.

basic.context: The book closes with a final account of sin, judgment, and atonement. David orders a census of his fighting men, counting the swordsmen of Israel and Judah. Even Joab objects, sensing something wrong in it, but the king insists. The sin seems to be pride and misplaced trust, numbering his military strength as though his security lay in the size of his army rather than in the LORD. When the count is done, David's conscience strikes him and he confesses he has sinned greatly and acted foolishly. The prophet Gad brings three options of judgment: famine, flight before enemies, or plague. David, refusing to fall into the hands of men, chooses to fall into the hand of the LORD, trusting His great mercy. A plague sweeps Israel, killing seventy thousand, until the destroying angel reaches Jerusalem and the LORD relents, saying, 'Enough.' The angel halts at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. David, seeing the people struck down, pleads as their shepherd that the judgment fall on him and his house, not on the innocent sheep. At God's command through Gad, David goes to build an altar on Araunah's threshing floor. Araunah offers to give it freely, but David insists on paying, refusing to offer God burnt offerings that cost him nothing. He builds the altar, offers sacrifices, and the plague is halted. That threshing floor becomes the site of the temple. The chapter raises questions about pride and misplaced trust, the cost of true worship, and the mercy that halts judgment through sacrifice.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative that ends the book on the note of atonement. The census sin is understood as pride and reliance on military might rather than on God, a temptation the law had guarded against by requiring a ransom with every counting, Exodus 30. The statement that the LORD stirred David, verse 1, read alongside 1 Chronicles 21:1 that Satan incited David, teaches God's sovereignty even over the occasion of judgment without making Him the author of David's sin. The chapter is descriptive; its enduring themes are honest confession, the greatness of God's mercy, the costliness of true worship, and the halting of judgment through sacrifice at the place that becomes the temple.
basic.originalLanguages: When the census is done, David's conscience strikes and he confesses, 'I have chata, sinned, greatly,' the same honest owning of guilt as after Bathsheba. Facing judgment, he chooses to fall into the hand of the LORD 'for His rachamim, His tender mercies, are great,' a word rooted in the yearning compassion of a parent's love. Sin honestly confessed and mercy deeply trusted frame the chapter, and the plague is halted precisely because the LORD relents in that great compassion.
basic.typology: The chapter is dense with types of Christ. David, the shepherd-king, offers himself for the sheep, 'let Your hand fall upon me,' foreshadowing the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. The plague is halted through sacrifice on an altar, pointing to the atonement that turns away wrath. And the threshing floor of Araunah becomes the temple mount, the very place of sacrifice, and lies near where Christ Himself would be sacrificed, so that the book ends at the ground where atonement is made and points to the cross.
basic.christ: The book's closing scene overflows with Christ. David the shepherd pleads that judgment fall on him, not the sheep, a shadow of Jesus, the Good Shepherd who truly bore the judgment His sheep deserved. The plague is stayed only through sacrifice on the altar, as God's wrath against sin is finally turned away only through the sacrifice of Christ. David's refusal to offer what costs him nothing points to the infinite cost of our redemption, paid not with silver but with the precious blood of Christ. And the threshing floor becomes the temple site, the place of atoning sacrifice, whose meaning is fulfilled at Calvary, where the true and final sacrifice halts the plague of sin forever.
basic.god: God is sovereign even over the occasion of judgment, yet never the author of David's sin; He is the holy Judge whose anger against sin is real, sending the plague, and the merciful Lord who relents and says 'Enough' when the angel reaches Jerusalem. David rightly trusts God's great mercy over the mercilessness of men. Above all, God is the one who provides the place and means of atonement, halting judgment through sacrifice, revealing a God whose justice and mercy meet at the altar, and pointing to the cross where they meet perfectly.
basic.crossReferences: First Chronicles 21 is the parallel account, adding that Satan incited David and identifying the site as the temple mount. Exodus 30 required a ransom whenever Israel was counted, illuminating the census sin. John 10 presents Christ as the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. And Second Chronicles 3 identifies Araunah's threshing floor as the site of Solomon's temple.
basic.oneStory: The book ends where it must, at the place of atonement. David's proud census brings judgment, but the shepherd-king offers himself for the sheep, God's great mercy relents, and the plague is halted through sacrifice on the threshing floor that becomes the temple. This closing scene of wrath turned away through costly sacrifice points forward to Jesus, the Good Shepherd who bears His people's judgment and, by His own precious blood, halts the plague of sin forever.

context.literary:
This closing chapter answers the appendix's opening scene rather than merely following the previous two poems. Chapter 21 begins, there was a famine in the days of David for three years, and David sought the face of the LORD; chapter 24 begins, again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel. Both national crises are resolved only through a costly act at a sacred site, atoning burial rites in chapter 21 and a purchased altar here, so the six panels of the appendix form a genuine ring, judgment and atonement bracketing two poems of praise and prophecy at the center.

Threes recur throughout this final scene almost as a structural signature. Gad offers three choices, famine, flight, or plague, each itself measured in units of three, years, months, or days. The census takes nine months and twenty days, a period built from that same number. Even the narrative's three movements, the count and the confession, the plague and the plea, the altar and its answer, echo this same patterning, suggesting a deliberate literary shape rather than mere coincidence in the underlying events.

The chapter's real center of gravity, however, is the single verse where David pleads as shepherd for his sheep, verse 17. Everything before it explains why judgment fell; everything after it explains how judgment was halted, and the shepherd's plea is the pivot joining the two, the exact point where a king's guilt becomes a king's intercession.
context.historical:
A census in the ancient Near East was rarely neutral information gathering. It was the essential first step toward conscription and forced labor, and a king who could number his troops precisely was a king preparing either for war or for the kind of large scale building projects that required corvee labor, the very demands Solomon would later impose, 1 Kings 5:13 to 14. Even Joab, no model of piety elsewhere in these books, senses that counting the fighting men this way risks treating Israel's strength as a resource to be managed rather than a gift from the LORD to be trusted.

The route Joab's officers traveled, Aroer, Gilead, the approaches to Tyre and Sidon, down through the Negev to Beersheba, sketches almost the full extent of the territory described in David's earlier conquests, chapter 8, so the census is not merely domestic bookkeeping but an inventory of empire.

Threshing floors sat deliberately on exposed, elevated ground where prevailing winds could carry the chaff away during winnowing, which is exactly why Araunah's floor, on the hill north of the old city of David, later became the site chosen for Solomon's temple, a location already naturally suited to public, open air use. The sum David finally pays, fifty shekels of silver, roughly a pound and a quarter, differs from the six hundred shekels of gold Chronicles records for what it calls the site, a difference most naturally explained as payment for the threshing floor and oxen alone here against a larger purchase of the surrounding hill itself in the fuller account, rather than a genuine contradiction between the two records.
context.canonical:
The threshing floor purchased here becomes, by explicit later record, the very ground on which Solomon builds the temple, 2 Chronicles 3:1, and that same mountain, Moriah, had already carried sacred weight nearly a thousand years earlier when Abraham was told to offer Isaac there, and instead offered a ram caught in a thicket, naming the place the LORD Will Provide, Genesis 22:14. One hill therefore carries three separate acts of substitutionary provision across the whole Old Testament, a ram in Abraham's place, a plague halted in Israel's place, and finally a temple built for sacrifice to continue there for centuries.

The unresolved tension of verse 1, the LORD stirred David against them, against the parallel account in 1 Chronicles 21:1, Satan incited David, sits alongside other Scripture passages that hold divine sovereignty and a real tempter's activity together without collapsing one into the other, most famously the opening chapters of Job, where the accuser acts only within limits God Himself sets.

David's insistence on paying full price rather than accepting a free gift echoes an older episode, Abraham likewise refusing to accept anything free from the king of Sodom, lest anyone say, I have made Abram rich, Genesis 14:23, both men insisting that what they offer to God, or keep for themselves before Him, must not look like charity accepted rather than sacrifice made.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The historian ends the entire account of David's reign not with his death, which is deliberately reserved for the opening of 1 Kings, but with smoke rising from an altar on a specific hill. That choice is itself the argument. Whatever David's story has been, ambition, adultery, murder, civil war, family catastrophe, its final word is neither tragedy nor triumph but atonement, God's anger answered by sacrifice rather than by the destruction the people's own guilt, and the king's, had actually earned.

The author also wants a later audience, quite plausibly one that had lost access to its own temple in exile, to see precisely where that temple's ground came from, not a conquest, not an inheritance, but a purchase made in the middle of a national emergency by a repentant king who refused to let atonement cost him nothing. Whatever became of the temple building itself, the ground beneath it was secured through confession, intercession, and costly obedience, and that founding logic, the author implies, remains true even when the building is gone.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This chapter describes one specific sin, one specific judgment, and one specific act of atonement, tied to a particular census, a particular threshing floor, and a particular ancient law about ransom money, Exodus 30:11 to 16. It is not a general prohibition on counting people, since censuses appear elsewhere in Scripture without any hint of wrongdoing, Numbers 1, and it is not a formula guaranteeing that any plague can be halted by any altar built anywhere.

What does transfer as lasting instruction is the pattern beneath the specifics, honest and immediate confession rather than excuse, a preference for falling into God's hand rather than into human hands whenever judgment is unavoidable, and the conviction that worship offered to God must cost the worshiper something real. David's insistence on paying full price rather than receiving Araunah's gift for free is not a rule that every offering must be purchased, but it is a permanent challenge to any worship that has quietly become convenient rather than costly.

debates.question: Who incited David to take the census, since 2 Samuel says the LORD and 1 Chronicles says Satan?

views.label: God's sovereign overruling working through a real tempter
views.case: Second Samuel 24:1 says the LORD, whose anger burned against Israel, stirred David, while 1 Chronicles 21:1 says Satan incited him; Scripture holds these together as it does with Job, where Satan acts only within God's sovereign permission; God, righteously angry with Israel, sovereignly ordained the occasion of judgment and permitted Satan to tempt David, yet David remains fully responsible, confessing 'I have sinned greatly,' so God's sovereignty and Satan's real agency and David's guilt all stand together without making God the author of sin.

views.label: Complementary perspectives on one event
views.case: Others stress that the two accounts give different vantage points on the same event, the ultimate divine purpose and the immediate satanic instigation, much as the cross was both God's set plan and the work of wicked hands, Acts 2:23; on this reading the texts are not in conflict but layered, teaching that God can use even a tempter's assault to accomplish His righteous ends while the human agent bears the guilt of his own choice.

debates.bearing: Both readings uphold God's sovereignty, Satan's genuine but permitted agency, and David's full moral responsibility, guarding against the error of making God the author of evil while affirming that nothing, not even judgment through a tempter, lies outside God's rule, a mystery finally illumined at the cross.

debates.question: Why does the plague fall on the whole nation rather than on David alone, since the census was his sin?

views.label: Covenantal solidarity between king and people
views.case: The chapter opens with the LORD's anger already burning against Israel for reasons the text never states directly, before David's census is even mentioned, verse 1, suggesting the nation stood under some prior, unspecified guilt for which the census became the occasion rather than the sole cause of judgment. Ancient Israel regularly experienced consequence corporately, as with Achan's sin bringing defeat on the whole army, Joshua 7, since a king's actions and a people's standing before God were never treated as separable.

views.label: The census itself was the specific offense that exposed the nation
views.case: Others focus on Exodus 30:11 to 16, which required atonement money whenever Israel's men were numbered precisely so that a census would never become an act of counting national strength apart from trusting the LORD who fights for His people. On this reading David's specific failure to collect that ransom is what brought guilt on the very men being counted, since they, not merely David, were the ones being numbered as though security lay in their own numbers.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that Scripture treats king and people as bound together under one covenant, so that a king's sin never stays merely private, and both anticipate the chapter's own resolution, judgment that could have justly fallen on the whole nation is instead halted through the substitutionary intercession and sacrifice of the one representative head, a pattern the New Testament will develop fully in Christ, Romans 5:12 to 19.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond chata and rachamim already named, several other words deepen the closing scene. David's confession pairs sin with folly, I have sinned greatly, and I have acted very foolishly, using two distinct categories of wrongdoing together, guilt before God and plain practical senselessness, as though David wants no reader to imagine his census was merely a private spiritual lapse rather than also an obviously reckless act any observer, like Joab, could see coming.

When the LORD relents, verse 16, the verb is nacham, a term Scripture also uses of God being grieved over human wickedness before the flood, Genesis 6:6, and of God relenting from the destruction announced against Nineveh, Jonah 3:10. The word pictures a genuine, responsive turning in God's dealings with people, not because God's character changes, but because He relates to repentance and intercession as real factors in how judgment unfolds, exactly what David's plea and Araunah's threshing floor together bring about here.

The altar David builds is a mizbeach, a word built directly on the verb to slaughter, so that the Hebrew name for the very structure of worship keeps sacrificial death built into its own meaning; there is, linguistically, no such thing as a bloodless mizbeach in Israel's vocabulary. And the ground it stands on is a goren, a threshing floor, ordinary agricultural machinery turned overnight into the holiest site David's own reign ever secures, a reminder that Israel's worship was never confined to specially built shrines but could consecrate the most working, everyday ground the moment God directed it.

Finally, 1 Chronicles names the tempter behind this whole episode satan, the adversary or accuser, a common Hebrew noun before it ever became, in later usage, the proper name of the ultimate opponent of God's people, and its presence in the parallel account shows Israel already understood real spiritual opposition standing behind at least some of David's own worst decisions.

One further pairing rewards attention. David's oxen are offered as an olah, a burnt offering wholly given up in smoke, and as shelamim, peace offerings shared afterward in a meal. The two Hebrew categories name two different transactions in a single act of worship, one that surrenders everything to God and one that restores table fellowship with Him, so that the very vocabulary of the sacrifice already anticipates a worship that both answers wrath and repairs relationship in a single motion.

typology.type: David the shepherd king pleading, let Your hand fall upon me, verse 17
typology.fulfillment: David offers himself in words alone, and the plague is in fact halted before it can touch him. Ezekiel later promises that the LORD Himself would come as shepherd to seek the lost and gather the scattered, Ezekiel 34:11 to 16, a promise realized when Jesus, the good shepherd, actually lays down His life for the sheep rather than merely offering to, John 10:11, and receives the very judgment David could only volunteer for and never actually bear.

typology.type: The angel halted at the threshing floor, judgment stopped short of the city, verse 16
typology.fulfillment: The destroying angel stops precisely at the site where sacrifice is about to be offered, a scene that closely mirrors Aaron standing with his censer between the living and the dead while a plague against Israel is halted, Numbers 16:46 to 48. Both scenes anticipate the cross, where wrath that had justly begun against a guilty people is halted, not by an appeal to leniency, but by an actual atoning act interposed between judgment and its intended target, Romans 3:25.

typology.type: The threshing floor of Araunah, later the temple mount, verses 18 to 25
typology.fulfillment: The same hill where Abraham had once been told the LORD Will Provide, offering a ram in his son's place, Genesis 22:14, becomes the ground on which Solomon's temple rises, 2 Chronicles 3:1, the fixed site of Israel's sacrificial worship for centuries. Hebrews describes a greater sanctuary not made with hands, where Christ entered once for all having obtained eternal redemption, Hebrews 9:11 to 12, the reality this one small hill of substitutionary provision had been quietly rehearsing since Abraham's day.

typology.type: David's refusal to offer what costs him nothing, verse 24
typology.fulfillment: Fifty shekels of silver is a real but modest price for what David insists must still be paid rather than received free. Peter contrasts perishable things such as silver or gold with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or defect, 1 Peter 1:18 to 19, the true and finally sufficient price behind every lesser, partial payment an Old Testament worshiper could ever offer.

study.christ:
The hill beneath this chapter's altar is not new ground. Centuries earlier Abraham stood on this same Moriah with a bound son and a raised knife, until God provided a substitute at the last possible moment and Abraham named the place the LORD Will Provide, Genesis 22:14. David now stands on that provision's own ground, watching a different substitute, oxen and an altar rather than a ram in a thicket, halt a different judgment. What began as a single family's rescue becomes, a millennium later, a nation's rescue on the identical hill, before becoming, centuries after that, the whole world's rescue near that same city.

The logic binding every scene together is stated plainly elsewhere in Scripture, without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, Hebrews 9:22. David's altar cost him fifty shekels and the lives of sacrificial animals; it bought a temporary halt to a specific plague. The cross costs the Father His own Son, He made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and buys not a delay of judgment but its actual end for everyone joined to Christ by faith.

Paul elsewhere calls Christ our Passover lamb, already sacrificed for us, 1 Corinthians 5:7, language that reaches back past David's threshing floor altogether to Israel's very first substitutionary night in Egypt, and forward past Solomon's temple to the once for all sacrifice that needs no further building, no further altar, and no further plague to answer, because it has already answered every plague sin could ever bring.

The hill itself does not disappear from the story either. Solomon's temple stood there for centuries, was destroyed, rebuilt, and destroyed again, yet the final vision of Scripture pictures no temple at all standing in the eternal city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. The whole trajectory that begins with Abraham's ram and David's altar ends with a city that no longer needs either, since the God once approached through a sacrifice on a hill now simply dwells, without any barrier left, among His people.
study.god:
God's anger in this chapter is neither random nor unlimited. The plague runs from that morning until the appointed time, a set boundary rather than an open ended catastrophe, and it is stopped by God's own initiative the very moment it reaches Jerusalem, before David has even finished speaking his plea. Wrath in this chapter is real, but it is never out of God's own control, even at its most severe.

God also fixes the exact place where reconciliation will happen rather than leaving it to David's own invention. Gad does not tell David simply to build an altar somewhere convenient; he names Araunah's threshing floor specifically, the very spot where the destroying angel already stood, verse 16. God locates mercy at the precise point where judgment had just been arrested, refusing to let atonement become a vague, general gesture rather than a concrete meeting with the place wrath had reached.

The chapter also shows God receiving more than one kind of offering at once, burnt offerings, which are wholly given up and consumed, and peace offerings, which are shared and eaten in fellowship, verse 25. Wrath answered and fellowship restored happen together at the same altar in the same hour, a single event doing the double work of turning judgment aside and reopening relationship, rather than two separate acts spread across time.

Finally, this God relents, a word that describes His genuine responsiveness to confession and intercession without implying His character or purposes have changed. The same LORD who was angry enough to send a plague is moved by David's honest confession and his plea to bear the judgment himself, showing that God's wrath and God's readiness to be moved by repentance are not competing attributes needing to be balanced against each other but two sides of the same covenant faithfulness, on full display in the very last scene the book of 2 Samuel gives its readers.

crossReferences.note: The parallel account names Satan as the one who incited David, adding a layer this chapter leaves unstated, and largely matches the sequence of confession, choice of judgment, and plague, differing mainly in emphasis and in naming the tempter directly where 2 Samuel names only the LORD's anger.

The law given at Sinai required a ransom payment whenever Israel's fighting men were counted, precisely so a census could never become an act of trusting national strength rather than the LORD who actually wins Israel's battles, the very failure this chapter's census appears to repeat.

Abraham's substitute ram on this same Moriah hill, and his naming of the place the LORD Will Provide, gives the threshing floor David later buys a much older sacred history, one act of substitutionary provision preparing the ground, quite literally, for another nearly a thousand years afterward.

Aaron runs with a lit censer and stands between the living and the dead until a plague among Israel is halted, an earlier scene of atoning intercession that closely parallels the destroying angel stopped at Araunah's threshing floor once David's sacrifice is offered.

Solomon builds the temple on this same site, turning David's emergency altar into Israel's permanent, central place of sacrifice, so that the location secured under crisis in this chapter becomes the fixed address of Israelite worship for centuries afterward.

Nearly everything under the law is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, the underlying principle that explains why David's crisis could be resolved only through burnt offerings on an altar and not through confession or good intentions alone.

God making Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin on our behalf so that we might become His righteousness describes an exchange this chapter can only gesture toward, David offering animals and silver where the gospel finally offers God's own Son in the sinner's place.

Paul names Christ our Passover lamb, already sacrificed, tying every Old Testament substitutionary altar, including this one, to a single final sacrifice that ends the need for repeated offerings rather than adding one more temporary halt to judgment.

One man's sin bringing condemnation to many, answered by one man's obedience bringing life to many, gives theological shape to the puzzle of why an entire nation suffered for its king's census, and why one king's confession and sacrifice could turn that judgment aside for all of them.

study.oneStory:
This chapter closes 2 Samuel at exactly the place biblical theology says every true story must eventually arrive, a sacrifice that halts deserved judgment and reopens fellowship with God. The thread runs back through the whole book of beginnings, cherubim barring the way to Eden's tree of life after the first sin, Genesis 3:24, Abraham's substitute ram on this very same Moriah hill, Genesis 22:13 to 14, and forward from David's altar to Solomon's temple built on the identical ground, until finally to a hill near that same city where the true and final substitute is offered once for all.

The king who sinned by numbering his own strength ends the book pleading to bear judgment personally rather than let it fall on people who never chose his sin, an office no other king in this history fills so clearly, shepherd standing between his flock and deserved destruction. That office does not disappear when David's own reign ends a few verses later, in the opening of 1 Kings; it becomes the very shape later Scripture uses to describe the Messiah, one who is struck for the transgression of a people not His own.

And the story does not stop at the cross either. The temple built on this hill stood, fell, and was rebuilt more than once across the centuries that followed, each rebuilding a fresh reminder that the arrangement was always meant to be temporary, pointing beyond itself. Revelation's final vision pictures a city with no temple at all, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple, so that the whole long history running from a garden's guarded tree, through a mountain's ram, a king's altar, and a temple's repeated construction, ends not with another building but with God dwelling directly among a people who need no further sacrifice, no further plague, and no further threshing floor, because the one sacrifice that actually mattered has already been made.

quiz.q: What was sinful about David's census of the fighting men?

options.text: It reflected pride and misplaced trust in his military strength rather than in the LORD.
options.note: The sin lay in relying on numbers and might rather than on God, which even Joab sensed was wrong.

options.text: Counting people was always forbidden under any circumstances.
options.note: Counting itself was not absolutely forbidden; the law allowed it with a ransom, and the sin here was the pride and misplaced trust behind it.

options.text: It showed David trusting in his army instead of in God.
options.note: True, but this option omits the element of pride and that the law required a ransom at every counting, which was neglected.

options.text: David was jealous of Joab's command of the army.
options.note: The issue was David's reliance on numbers, not jealousy of Joab, who actually objected to the census.

quiz.q: Why does David choose to fall into the hand of the LORD rather than into the hands of men?

options.text: Because the LORD's mercies are great, so he trusts God's compassion over the mercilessness of men.
options.note: Verse 14 records David's trust in God's great mercy in choosing his judgment.

options.text: Because he thought God's judgment would be the least painful option.
options.note: David's reason is God's great mercy, not that the plague would hurt least; the plague was severe.

options.text: Because he preferred to trust God's compassion rather than human cruelty.
options.note: True, but this option omits the specific reason he gives, that the LORD's mercies are great.

options.text: Because Gad the prophet told him which option to choose.
options.note: Gad presented the options; David himself chose, trusting God's mercy, not on Gad's instruction.

quiz.q: What does David plead when he sees the plague striking the people?

options.text: That the judgment fall on him and his house, since he the shepherd sinned, not the innocent sheep.
options.note: Verse 17 records David's shepherd's plea to bear the judgment for his people.

options.text: That God spare him personally while judging the guilty people.
options.note: The opposite; David asks that the judgment fall on him, not the people.

options.text: That God's hand fall on him rather than on the people.
options.note: True, but this option omits the tender shepherd-and-sheep imagery that makes the plea a foreshadowing of Christ.

options.text: That Joab be punished for carrying out the census.
options.note: David takes the blame himself as the shepherd; he does not shift it to Joab, who had objected.

quiz.q: Why does David insist on paying Araunah for the threshing floor and oxen?

options.text: Because he will not offer the LORD burnt offerings that cost him nothing.
options.note: Verse 24 records David's refusal to offer a costless sacrifice.

options.text: Because Araunah demanded a high price for his property.
options.note: Araunah offered it all for free; it was David who insisted on paying.

options.text: Because true worship should cost the worshiper something.
options.note: True, but this option generalizes David's specific words about not offering what costs him nothing.

options.text: Because the law required the king to buy any altar site.
options.note: No such law is cited; David acts from conviction that his offering must be costly, not from a legal requirement.

quiz.q: How does the book's closing scene point to Christ?

options.text: The shepherd offers himself for the sheep and judgment is halted through costly sacrifice on the future temple site, foreshadowing the cross.
options.note: The shepherd's plea, the atoning sacrifice, and the temple site all point to Christ, John 10:11 and Romans 3:25.

options.text: It teaches that plagues can always be stopped by building altars.
options.note: The point is atonement pointing to Christ, not a formula for stopping plagues.

options.text: It shows judgment turned away through sacrifice, fulfilled at Calvary.
options.note: True, but this option omits the shepherd offering himself for the sheep, a striking foreshadowing of Christ.

options.text: It proves that David earned forgiveness by his generous payment.
options.note: The plague is halted by God's mercy through sacrifice, not by David earning forgiveness with money.

questions: David's census sprang from trusting in his own strength and numbers. Where are you tempted to find your security in resources, achievements, or influence rather than in God?
When convicted, David honestly confessed, 'I have sinned greatly.' How quick are you to own your sin plainly before God rather than excusing or minimizing it?
David chose to fall into the hand of the LORD because His mercies are great. How does trusting in the depth of God's compassion change the way you face the consequences of your failures?
David refused to offer God anything that cost him nothing. Where might your worship or service to God have become convenient and costless, and what would costly devotion look like?

The shepherd-king offered himself for the sheep, foreshadowing Christ who truly bore our judgment. How does it move you that the Good Shepherd laid down His life so the plague of sin could be halted for you forever?

translationNotes.note: That 'the LORD stirred up David' is complemented by 1 Chronicles 21:1, 'Satan incited David'; Scripture holds God's sovereign overruling and Satan's real, permitted agency together, as in Job, without making God the author of David's sin, which David fully owns.

The BSB reads 'three years of famine' following the Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 21:12, while the Hebrew here reads 'seven years'; the three-year reading matches the parallel and the threefold pattern of the options.

The BSB footnote notes that Araunah is called Ornan in 1 Chronicles 21:15; his threshing floor becomes the site of Solomon's temple on Mount Moriah, 2 Chronicles 3:1, so the book ends at the place of atonement.
